title: Digital data
everyday: How numbers, letters and pictures are stored as 0s and 1s.

screens.title: Bits, nibbles and bytes: the switches inside a computer
screens.goal: I can say why computers use 0 and 1 and count the bits in a byte.

say: Every chip in a computer is packed with millions of tiny switches. Each switch is off or on.
A switch with only two states is cheap, fast and hard to get wrong. That is why computers count in 0 and 1.
Off is written as 0. On is written as 1. One switch, one 0 or 1, is a [[bit|1]].
A bit is the smallest thing a computer can store. Nothing is smaller than off or on.
Four bits together are a [[nibble|1]]. Eight bits together are a [[byte|1]].
A byte can hold one character, like the letter k or the digit 7. Every file is a long row of bytes.

picture.title: A wall plate with eight light switches
lines: Picture a wall plate with eight light switches in a row. Each switch is up or down, nothing in between.
That plate is a byte. One switch on its own is a bit. Four switches together make a nibble.
A computer holds billions of these plates. Every photo, song and message is stored as switches.
match: One light switch, up or down
The whole plate of eight switches
picture.breaks: Real switches are big and slow. The switches in a chip are smaller than a germ. They flip billions of times a second.

play.title: Flip the eight switches
play.lead: Tap any switch to flip it. Count how many are on. Four switches is one nibble, eight is one byte.

exam.say: A bit is a binary digit. It can only take on the values 0 or 1. It is the smallest unit of storage in a computer system. A nibble is 4 bits. A byte is 8 bits.

try.stem: Pick TRUE or FALSE for each statement.

rows: Half a byte is called a nibble.

try.why: A nibble is four bits, half a byte. A bit is only ever 0 or 1.

screens.title: Binary to denary: add the headings that have a 1
screens.goal: I can read an 8-bit binary pattern and say what denary number it is, with working.

say: The numbers you count with every day are [[denary|1]] numbers. Denary uses ten digits, 0 to 9.
A computer counts with only two digits, 0 and 1. That is [[binary|1]].
Each bit in a byte has a heading. From the right, the headings are 1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32, 64 and 128.
Each heading is double the one to its right. A 1 under a heading means that heading is counted.
To turn a byte into denary, add up the headings that have a 1 under them. Ignore the 0s.

anim.title: Turn 10110101 into denary, step by step
anim.lead: Press Next to see the working the examiner wants to see. Every step adds one thing to the table.
steps: Start by writing the eight headings in a row. Begin with 128 on the left and halve each time.
Copy the bits under the headings, one bit under each heading. Here the pattern is 10110101.
Mark every heading that has a 1 under it. Headings with a 0 under them score nothing.
Write those headings as an addition. 128 + 32 + 16 + 4 + 1.
Add them up. 128 + 32 + 16 + 4 + 1 = 181. So 10110101 is 181 in denary.

picture.title: A ruler with eight marks
lines: Picture a ruler where the marks are not evenly spaced. The marks read 128, 64, 32, 16, 8, 4, 2 and 1.
Under each mark is a switch. Turn a switch on and you add that mark to the total.
With all eight switches on you get 255. With all off you get 0. Every number between has its own pattern.
match: A place value, also called a heading
A switch turned on under a mark
Adding up the marks you switched on
The biggest number one byte can hold
picture.breaks: A real ruler is evenly spaced. This one doubles at every mark, and that doubling is what makes binary work.

play.title: Your turn: binary to denary
play.lead: A random byte appears. Write the headings in your head, add the ones with a 1, type the total. Check it, then press Another one.

exam.say: Write the place values 128, 64, 32, 16, 8, 4, 2, 1 above the bits. Add the place values that have a 1 beneath them. Show the working, because the working earns a mark.
exam.src: 2021 Q6(b) mark scheme: conversion work, addition of results, 251

try.stem: What is the binary pattern 01011010 in denary?
try.why: The 1s sit under 64, 16, 8 and 2. Added up, 64 + 16 + 8 + 2 = 90.

screens.title: Denary to binary: can it be taken away?
screens.goal: I can turn any denary number up to 255 into eight bits and show my working.

say: Going the other way is a game of take away. Write the eight headings, then start at 128.
Ask one question at every heading. Can this heading be taken away from what I have left?
If it can, write a 1 under it and take it away. If it cannot, write a 0 and move on.
Keep going until the 1 heading. What you have left should be 0 when you finish.
Always write all eight bits, even when the first ones are 0.

anim.title: Turn 147 into binary, step by step
anim.lead: Press Next to ask the question at each heading. Watch the remainder fall to 0.
steps: Write the eight headings. Start with 147 as the amount left.
Can 128 be taken from 147? Yes. Write 1. 147 take away 128 leaves 19.
Can 64 be taken from 19? No. Write 0. 19 is still left.
Can 32 be taken from 19? No. Write 0. 19 is still left.
Can 16 be taken from 19? Yes. Write 1. 19 take away 16 leaves 3.
Can 8 be taken from 3? No. Write 0.
Can 4 be taken from 3? No. Write 0.
Can 2 be taken from 3? Yes. Write 1. 3 take away 2 leaves 1.
Can 1 be taken from 1? Yes. Write 1. Nothing is left, so 147 is 10010011.

blocks.watch: A pattern with fewer than eight bits can lose a mark. The 2022 paper gave one mark for 7 bits, not two. Write all eight.

play.title: Your turn: denary to binary
play.lead: A random number appears. Switch on the headings that fit, left to right, then check. The take away table shows after you check.

exam.say: Show conversion work. Divide by two or use place value, either is accepted. Then write the full 8-bit pattern.

try.stem: Which 8-bit pattern is the denary number 53?
try.why: 53 is 32 + 16 + 4 + 1. Switch on 32, 16, 4 and 1 and you get 00110101.

screens.title: Units of storage: bit to terabyte
screens.goal: I can order the storage units and pick the largest from a mixed list.

say: A byte is tiny. One phone photo is about three million bytes. So bigger units are needed.
A [[kilobyte|1]] is 1,024 bytes. A [[megabyte|1]] is 1,024 kilobytes.
A [[gigabyte|1]] is 1,024 megabytes. A [[terabyte|1]] is 1,024 gigabytes.
Why 1,024 and not 1,000? Because 1,024 is 2 multiplied by itself ten times. Computers like doubling.
In rough working, 1,000 is close enough and the paper accepts it. So 2 terabytes is about 2,000 gigabytes.

picture.title: A staircase of boxes
lines: Picture a staircase. On the bottom step sits a bit. One step up, four bits make a nibble, then eight make a byte.
Each step above holds 1,024 of the step below. Kilobyte, megabyte, gigabyte, terabyte.
A text message sits on the kilobyte step. A song is a few megabytes. A film is a few gigabytes. A hard disk is terabytes.
picture.breaks: The staircase does not stop at terabyte. Petabytes and more exist, but the GCSE paper stops here.

play.title: Climb the storage staircase
play.lead: Tap a step to see how big it is and what fits on it.

exam.say: Smallest to largest: bit, nibble, byte, kilobyte, megabyte, gigabyte, terabyte. A nibble is 4 bits. A byte is 8 bits.

parts.stem: Match each unit to its size.
parts.why: Four bits, eight bits, then 1,024 of the step below at every step up.

parts.stem: Which of these is the largest amount of storage?
parts.why: A terabyte is 1,024 gigabytes, so even 2 terabytes beats 900 gigabytes. Compare the units first, then the numbers.

screens.title: Hexadecimal: what it is and where it is used
screens.goal: I can say what hex is, how it uses nibbles and where it is used.

say: Long binary patterns are hard to read and easy to miscopy. So people use [[hexadecimal|1]], hex for short.
Hex counts in sixteens. It has sixteen digits: 0 to 9, then A, B, C, D, E and F.
A stands for 10, B for 11 and C for 12. D is 13, E is 14 and F is 15.
Here is the trick. One hex digit stands for exactly one nibble, four bits.
So a byte is just two hex digits. 10010011 becomes 93. Much shorter and easier to read.
Hex is used for colour codes on web pages, memory addresses and some character codes. It takes fewer digits than binary.

picture.title: A nickname for every nibble
lines: Think of each nibble as a person with a long full name, like 1011. Hex gives that person a one-letter nickname, B.
Sixteen nibbles, sixteen nicknames. 0000 is 0, 1001 is 9, 1010 is A, 1111 is F.
A web colour like #FF6600 is three bytes written as nicknames. FF is full red, 66 is some green, 00 is no blue.
match: Three bytes of colour, written in hex
picture.breaks: A nickname can be anything you like. A hex digit always stands for the same four bits, in every computer, everywhere.

play.title: Watch the hex readout
play.lead: Flip switches and watch the hex readout. Each hex digit watches only its own four switches.

exam.say: Hexadecimal is a base 16 number system. It uses the digits 0 to 9 and the letters A to F. Programmers use it to shorten long binary patterns: one hex digit stands for four bits. Uses: colour codes, memory addresses, Unicode characters, assembly language. Advantage over binary: large numbers can be represented using fewer digits. That makes them more readable and less likely to be miscopied.

try.stem: Match each nibble to its hex digit.
try.why: 1010 is 10, which is A. 1111 is 15, which is F. 0011 is 3. 1100 is 12, which is C.

screens.title: Hex and binary: one hex digit for each nibble
screens.goal: I can change a byte into two hex digits and back again.

say: Binary to hex is a split. Cut the byte into two nibbles, four bits on the left and four on the right.
Give each nibble its own value using the headings 8, 4, 2, 1. Then write that value as one hex digit.
Values 0 to 9 stay as digits. 10 to 15 become the letters A to F.
Hex to binary is the same trip backwards. Each hex digit becomes four bits. Put the two nibbles side by side.

anim.title: 11111011 to hex, then A9 back to binary
anim.lead: Press Next to split the byte, name each nibble, then go the other way.
steps: Here is the byte 11111011. Cut it in the middle into two nibbles.
The left nibble is 1111. Using 8, 4, 2, 1 that is 8 + 4 + 2 + 1 = 15. Fifteen is F.
The right nibble is 1011. That is 8 + 2 + 1 = 11. Eleven is B.
Write the two hex digits side by side. 11111011 is FB in hexadecimal.
Now the other way. The hex code A9 has two digits, A and 9.
A is 10. With headings 8, 4, 2, 1 that is 8 + 2, so the nibble is 1010.
9 is 8 + 1, so the nibble is 1001.
Put the nibbles side by side. A9 is 10101001 in binary.

play.title: Your turn: hex and binary
play.lead: The questions take turns, byte to hex and hex to byte. Check each one, then press Another one.

exam.say: Split the bit pattern into two nibbles. Convert each nibble to one hex digit. Hex to binary: convert each hex digit to 4 bits. Show the nibbles as working.

try.stem: What is the byte 10101100 in hexadecimal?
try.why: Split it: 1010 is 10, which is A, and 1100 is 12, which is C. So AC.

screens.title: Hex and denary: go through binary, then check with sixteens
screens.goal: I can change a hex code into denary and a denary number into hex, with working.

say: Hex to denary has a safe route. Change each hex digit into four bits, then add the headings as on screen 2.
There is also a quick check. The left hex digit counts sixteens and the right hex digit counts ones.
So E3 is 14 sixteens plus 3 ones. 14 × 16 = 224, and 224 + 3 = 227.
Denary to hex goes the other way. Change the number into eight bits, then split into nibbles.
Or divide by 16. The answer is the left digit and the remainder is the right digit.

anim.title: E3 to denary two ways
anim.lead: Press Next to take the binary route, then check the answer with sixteens.
steps: Start with the hex code E3. E is one digit and 3 is the other.
E is 14. In four bits, 14 is 8 + 4 + 2, so 1110.
3 is 2 + 1, so the nibble is 0011. Together, E3 is 11100011.
Write the eight headings over the byte and add the ones with a 1. 128 + 64 + 32 + 2 + 1.
Check with sixteens. E is 14, and 14 × 16 = 224. Add the 3 ones: 224 + 3 = 227. It matches.

blocks.watch: Hex letters can be big or small. 9b and 9B are the same answer. But never mix a hex digit into denary working, or the examiner cannot follow it.

play.title: Your turn: hex and denary
play.lead: The questions take turns, hex to denary and denary to hex. Type your answer and check it. The working shows after.

exam.say: For denary to hex, show the base 16 working or the binary conversion. Then write each hex digit. For hex to denary, show each hex digit as 4 bits or the place value working. The working earns a mark.
exam.src: 2021 Q6(d), 2023 Q7(c)(i) and 2025 Q4(a)(ii) mark schemes

try.stem: What is the hex code FF in denary?
try.why: F is 15. Fifteen sixteens are 240. Add fifteen ones and you get 255. FF is also 11111111, the biggest byte.

screens.title: Adding two bytes and spotting overflow
screens.goal: I can add two bytes with carries and say what overflow does to the answer.

say: Adding binary works like adding denary, column by column from the right. There are four facts to know.
0 plus 0 is 0. 0 plus 1 is 1. 1 plus 1 is 10, so write 0 and carry 1.
1 plus 1 plus 1 is 11, so write 1 and carry 1.
Write the carry above the next column to the left. Then add that column, carry included.
A byte has eight columns. If the last carry needs a ninth column, that is [[overflow|1]].

anim.title: Add 01011011 and 00110111, then see overflow
anim.lead: Press Next to add one column at a time, right to left. Watch where the carries go.
steps: Write the two bytes one above the other, headings on top. Start at the right hand column.
Column 1: 1 + 1 = 10. Write 0 and carry 1 into the next column.
Column 2: 1 + 1 + 1 = 11. Write 1 and carry 1.
Column 3: 0 + 1 + 1 = 10. Write 0 and carry 1.
Column 4: 1 + 0 + 1 = 10. Write 0 and carry 1.
Column 5: 1 + 1 + 1 = 11. Write 1 and carry 1.
Column 6: 0 + 1 + 1 = 10. Write 0 and carry 1.
Column 7: 1 + 0 + 1 = 10. Write 0 and carry 1.
Column 8: 0 + 0 + 1 = 1. Write 1 with no carry. The answer is 10010010, which is 146.
Now 11100011 + 01101110. The last column carries a 1 into a ninth column. A byte has no ninth column, so this is overflow.
The ninth bit is lost. The byte shows 01010001, which is 81, but the true total is 337. The answer is wrong.

picture.title: A car's mileage counter rolling over
lines: An old car has a mileage counter with six digit wheels. It can show up to 999999.
Drive one more mile and every wheel rolls to 0. The counter says 000000. The car did not go back in time.
The million was lost because there was no seventh wheel. A byte has eight wheels, and the ninth bit is that lost million.
match: The ninth bit, which is overflow
The counter showing a tiny number
picture.breaks: A mileage counter rolls over quietly. The exam wants you to circle the overflow bit so the examiner sees you spotted it.

play.title: Add two bytes live
play.lead: Tap any bit in the two top rows to flip it. Watch the carry row, the result and the ninth bit.

exam.say: The magnitude of the number exceeds the range. The value from the addition is outside the range the bit pattern can store. The overflow digit is dropped, ignored or lost. The result may be incorrect.

parts.stem: Fill the gaps using the word bank.

surface.text: When 11111111 and 00000001 are added, the result needs {1} bits. The extra bit is called {2}. It is {3}, so the stored result is {4}.

parts.why: 255 plus 1 is 256, which needs nine bits. The ninth bit is overflow, it is lost, and the byte shows 0.

parts.stem: Pick TRUE or FALSE for each statement about overflow.

rows: Overflow happens when the total needs more bits than the byte has.
The extra bit is kept in a ninth column of the byte.
The stored answer is smaller than the true total.
Overflow means the two bytes were added wrongly.

parts.why: The sum was done right, but a byte has only eight columns. The ninth bit is lost, so the stored answer is wrong and too small.

screens.title: ASCII and Unicode: a number for every character
screens.goal: I can say what ASCII is, how many codes it has and why Unicode came.

say: Letters, digits and symbols are called characters. A computer stores each character as a number.
The first big agreed list of these numbers was [[ASCII|1]]. It stands for American Standard Code for Information Interchange.
The original ASCII used 7 bits for each character. Seven bits give 128 different codes.
Extended ASCII used 8 bits, a full byte. Eight bits give 256 codes, but that is still not enough.
Different regions filled the extra codes differently, so a file could show the wrong letters elsewhere.
[[Unicode|1]] fixes this with a code for every character in every language, emoji included.
The first 128 Unicode codes are the ASCII codes, so old text still works. Unicode characters need more storage.

picture.title: Two phone books
lines: ASCII is a thin phone book for one small town. Every person has a number, and there is room for 256 names.
Unicode is the phone book for the whole world. Every letter in every language has its own number, emoji too.
The world book kept every number from the town book. Look up A and you get 65 in both.
match: The code number for a character
The town book sitting inside the world book
ASCII is a subset of Unicode
picture.breaks: A phone book is printed once. Unicode keeps growing, with new emoji added most years.

play.title: Type a character, see its code
play.lead: Type a letter, a digit or an emoji. See the number the computer stores for it.

exam.say: ASCII stands for American Standard Code for Information Interchange. 7-bit ASCII represents 128 characters and 8-bit ASCII represents 256 characters. Unicode was introduced because ASCII could not represent the characters of every language. The extended codes also clashed between regions. Unicode represents every character in every language, including emoji. ASCII is the first part of Unicode. Unicode characters need more bits, so more storage.
exam.src: 2019 Q7(a), 2023 Q1(a) and 2025 Q4(d) mark schemes

try.stem: Pick TRUE or FALSE for each statement about character codes.

rows: The original ASCII table used seven bits for each character.
Unicode has a code for the characters of every language.
A Unicode character can need more storage than an ASCII one.

try.why: Seven bits give 128 codes and eight bits give 256. Unicode covers every language, and its characters can take more bits.

screens.title: Data types: which kind of value is it?
screens.goal: I can name the data types and choose the right one for any variable.

say: Every piece of data in a program has a [[data type|1]]. The type tells the computer what kind of thing it is holding.
An [[integer|1]] is a whole number, positive or negative, with no decimal part. A count of goals is an integer.
A [[real|1]] number can have a decimal part. A price like 1.99 is real. Programmers also say double or float.
A [[character|1]] is one single letter, digit or symbol, like the grade B.
A [[string|1]] is a run of characters, like a name or a postcode. A postcode with digits in it is still a string.
A [[Boolean|1]] holds only true or false. Has the pupil passed? True or false.
A [[date/time|1]] type holds a date, a time, or both. The computer can then add days or compare two times.
A name like passFail or isValid is a clue. A yes or no answer is a Boolean.

picture.title: Labelled jars on a shelf
lines: Picture a shelf of jars, each with a label saying what goes inside. One jar says whole numbers only.
Another says numbers with decimal points. Another says one letter only. Another says words.
One jar holds a single coin, heads or tails. One holds a calendar page. Put a price in the whole numbers jar and the pennies fall off.
match: Real, also called double or float
picture.breaks: You could force a word into a real jar. The computer refuses to put a word into an integer and shows an error instead.

code.title: Six variables, six data types
lines: string studentName = "Aoife Quinn";
double courseworkMark = 67.5;
char courseworkGrade = 'B';
bool passFail = true;
int goalsScored = 3;
DateTime examDate = new DateTime(2027, 5, 14);
parts: Text in double quotes. Any run of characters.
C# calls it double. It keeps the decimal part.
Only true or false, nothing else.
A whole number. No decimal point allowed.
A date and a time held in one value.
names: The data type for text. The exam word is string.
C# for a date and time.

exam.say: Integer: a whole number. Real, double or float: a number with a decimal part. Character or char: one character. String: text. Boolean or bool: true or false. Date/time: a date and a time.
exam.src: 2019 Q1(a), 2022 Q4(b)(ii) and 2025 Q3(b) mark schemes

parts.stem: Match each variable to the best data type.
parts.why: A count is an integer. Valid is true or false. A surname is text. A price has pence, so it is real.

parts.stem: A studio booking system stores the Category of each booking, such as Category 1. It stores hoursBooked as whole hours. Fill each gap with the most appropriate data type.
parts.why: Category holds words like Category 1, so it is a string. Whole hours are an integer.

screens.title: Boolean logic: AND, OR and NOT truth tables
screens.goal: I can work out AND, OR and NOT and fill every cell of a truth table.

say: Computers make decisions with three little words: AND, OR and NOT. Each one is a rule about 1s and 0s.
A [[truth table|1]] lists every possible input and the output the rule gives. Two inputs means four rows: 00, 01, 10, 11.
[[AND|1]] gives 1 only when both inputs are 1. [[OR|1]] gives 1 when either input is 1, or both.
[[NOT|1]] has one input and flips it. NOT 1 is 0 and NOT 0 is 1.
When a rule has brackets, work out the brackets first. Then apply the rule outside them.

picture.title: Two switches and a lamp
lines: A lamp is wired to two wall switches, A and B.
Wired as AND, the lamp lights only when both switches are on. Wired as OR, either switch alone lights it.
Wired as NOT on one switch, the lamp does the opposite. Switch off means lamp on.
match: The lamp does the opposite of its switch
breaks: Real switches can be half pressed or broken. A Boolean value is always exactly 0 or 1.

play.title: Two switches, one lamp
play.lead: Pick a rule, then flip switch A and switch B. Watch the lamp and the truth table row light up.

anim.title: Fill in NOT(P AND Q), row by row
anim.lead: Press Next to fill one row at a time. The brackets are worked out first, then NOT flips the answer.
steps: The paper gives P, Q and an empty column for NOT(P AND Q). Four rows cover every input.
Row 1: P is 0 and Q is 0. P AND Q is 0. NOT 0 is 1, so write 1.
Row 2: P is 0 and Q is 1. P AND Q is 0. NOT 0 is 1, so write 1.
Row 3: P is 1 and Q is 0. P AND Q is 0. NOT 0 is 1, so write 1.
Row 4: P is 1 and Q is 1. P AND Q is 1. NOT 1 is 0, so write 0.
Every cell is filled. The column reads 1, 1, 1, 0. Each cell earns its own mark.

exam.say: AND: the output is 1 only when all inputs are 1. OR: the output is 1 when any input is 1. NOT: the output is the opposite of the input. Work out any brackets first. Fill every empty cell. Each cell or column earns its own mark.
exam.src: 2019 Q8(e), 2023 Q1(c) and 2024 Q4(e) mark schemes

try.stem: A = 1 and C = 0. D is NOT C. E is A AND D. F is D OR E. Pick TRUE or FALSE for each line.
try.why: NOT 0 is 1, so D is 1. A AND D is 1 AND 1, so E is 1. D OR E is 1 OR 1, which is 1, so F is 1 not 0.
